name: Testosterone pellets (Testopel)

card.summary: Rice-grain testosterone implants placed under the skin for months-long TRT; an established medical option with observational and small-trial data.
card.note: Requires a minor in-office procedure; compounded pellets are not FDA-approved products.

quick.overview:
Testosterone pellets are small solid implants placed under the skin that release testosterone gradually. Testopel is the FDA-approved brand; the US approved implantable pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency, and they returned to wider clinical use in recent years.

They appeal to people who want to avoid frequent injections or daily gels. Published work consists mainly of observational studies and a few small trials, not long-term outcome trials.
quick.mechanism: Pellets are inserted subcutaneously, typically in the hip or buttock area, and slowly dissolve, releasing testosterone into the bloodstream over several months. Medication overviews list dosing every 3 to 6 months, with pellets in 50, 75, 100 and 200 mg strengths.
quick.risks: Because the pellets are implanted, a minor procedure is needed, and reported complications of implant procedures include infection and pellet extrusion. As with other testosterone therapy, effects include acne, raised red blood cell counts, sperm suppression and other systemic effects. Compounded pellets are not the same as the branded FDA-approved product.

lead: Testosterone pellets are small cylindrical implants of crystalline testosterone placed under the skin to provide sustained hormone release. Testopel is the branded product; a 2012 multi-institution study notes that the FDA approved implantable testosterone pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency syndrome, and that clinical use was limited until Testopel was reintroduced.[1] A review notes they were not marketed until 2008.[7]

The appearance connection runs through testosterone's effects: restoring levels in men with deficiency is associated with muscle maintenance and growth, and androgenic effects such as body hair, deeper voice and, in some people, acne and scalp hair loss.[4] Pellets appeal to people on testosterone therapy who want steady levels from an implant every 3 to 6 months instead of daily gel or frequent injections.[2][4]

Medication references list pellet doses of 150 to 1,200 mg every 3 to 6 months for men, in strengths of 50 to 200 mg per pellet.[4] Evidence consists of observational serum-level studies, patient-preference surveys and small randomised trials, mostly in men with diagnosed hypogonadism.[1][2][3] No published trials have examined pellets for appearance outcomes in healthy people.

paras: Pellets are used for testosterone replacement in men with deficiency [1]. A single-centre trial also compared compounded and branded pellets in men with testosterone deficiency [3]. A registered phase 1 trial tested pellets together with vitamins D and E in Peyronie's disease [6].

A multi-institution observational study combined databases from six academic centres to characterise serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion [1]. A randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial compared a compounded pellet (E100) with Testopel in men with testosterone deficiency to assess both safety and efficacy [3]. A further phase 3 registration compares Testopel with generic pellets in 75 men [5].

A review of pellet therapy describes decay kinetics, pituitary suppression and effects on other sex steroids following insertion, noting that older pharmacokinetic work was on a different formulation (Organon pellets) but informs Testopel.[7] A 1990 randomised study characterised pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of pellets in men.[8]

Older reports noted relatively high rates of pellet extrusion and infection with Organon pellets; a randomised trial in 1999 tested whether washing pellets to remove surface particles reduced extrusion.[9][10] A 2009 single-site retrospective analysis reported safety and limited efficacy data from patients treated with Testopel.[10]
A survey-based study of 175 men at an academic urology practice examined what led patients to start or stop pellets compared with gels and injections [2].

On T Nation, a 2010 thread asks for Testopel experiences and includes a user saying the quarterly implant was the least laborious method compared with gel, and another posting that he had used it for three years.[11] Another poster says insurance began accepting Testopel and compares costs of pellets from a compounding pharmacy.[12] Other users in the same communities favour injections or note high measured levels on pellets and discuss individual lab results.[13]

General testosterone therapy effects include acne, oily skin and hair loss, sperm suppression, and warnings related to cardiovascular events, prostate conditions and blood pressure; testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy [4]. Implantation is a minor surgical procedure, which makes procedure-related events such as infection a topic in the pellet literature.

Wikipedia lists common testosterone effects as acne, swelling and breast enlargement in men, with serious risks including liver toxicity and heart disease, and notes a February 2025 FDA label change that removed cardiovascular language from the boxed warning and added a blood pressure warning.[4] A 2021 case report examined Testopel therapy and laboratory assay interpretation.[14]

Pellets are offered through urology and hormone clinics and are also prepared by compounding pharmacies, which the 2023 trial compared against the branded product [3]. Testosterone is a controlled substance in the US [4].

Brand lists for testosterone products include Testopel among injections, gels and patches.[4] In the US it is Schedule III, in the UK Class C, and prescription-only in the EU.[4] Pellets are also used in transmasculine hormone therapy and are approved in the UK for postmenopausal women, according to Wikipedia.[4]

Observational data show serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion across six academic centres [1]. A 2023 randomised trial compared compounded and branded pellets [3], and a phase 3 trial (NCT04523480, 75 men, completed) compared Testopel with generic pellets [5]. A phase 1 trial (NCT01578473, 75 participants) tested pellets for Peyronie's disease [6]. No studies found for appearance or physique outcomes in healthy people.
Earlier trials include the 1999 randomised extrusion study and the 1990 pharmacokinetic randomised trial; men's contraception trials have also used testosterone pellets with progestins.[8][9][15]

timeline.event: FDA approves implantable testosterone pellets for testosterone deficiency [1].
Randomised study of pellet pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in men.[8]
Testopel marketed in the US after the 1972 approval.[7]
Six-institution observational study of Testopel serum levels published [1].
Randomised trial compares compounded and branded pellets [3].

lore.intro: Testopel is discussed on T Nation by men comparing TRT delivery methods; threads cover convenience, cost and experience with compounded pellets.[11][12]

claims.claim: Pellets are the least laborious way to do TRT
claims.believers: A poster described an implant every three months as avoiding daily gel and injections.[11]
claims.experts: Reviews describe pellets as long-acting options with a minor insertion procedure and complications such as extrusion and infection.[7][9]

claims.claim: Pellets are less controllable than injections
claims.believers: Some users moved to frequent injections after trying other protocols, discussing dose adjustment.[12]
claims.experts: Published observational studies characterise serum testosterone after insertion across centres.[1]

claims.claim: Compounded pellets are equivalent to branded Testopel
claims.believers: Users report using custom pellets from compounding pharmacies for cost reasons.[12]
claims.experts: A 2023 single-centre randomised trial compared a compounded pellet with Testopel on efficacy and safety.[3]

Muscle, body composition and androgen-dependent features supported while levels are maintained
angle.text: For people already prescribed testosterone, pellets are one delivery format. Testosterone's recognised effects include muscle growth and androgenic traits, so people on therapy in physique communities discuss pellets as a low-maintenance way to keep levels steady.
